Q: Synchronizing requests on body property value A:

The database is the answer. Specifically, a database in SERIALIZABLE mode:

  1. Now any other system that interacts with the DB can use the same concurrency safety mechanism. Whereas if you do it in java, it is not possible for any code other than the 1 java process to do this. And sometimes that 'other system' is you, on the command line, doing some admin work. It's nice to know you don't have to shut down your JVM to avoid causing a race condition between your admin work and some user using the service.
  2. Now you can shard your JVMs (have more than 1 JVM handling requests, as long as there is just the one DB. There are ways to make it so that you can have multiple DB systems too, but that's much more complicated).
  3. You need transactions in your DB anyway. It's annoying and confusing to have two separate systems that both can and sometimes do supply concurrent safety mechanisms. Much simpler to have just one.
  4. DB transactions are easier to reason about. The concept (just try it optimistically, and check on commit, throwing an exception to indicate - nope, conflict, rerun your code) is so popular, programming languages are trying to introduce it into their systems. In general the model is more 'constructable' - when you glue separate bits of code into a whole, with a serializable db concurrency model, it's less likely that the act of glueing things together breaks concurrency rules. Whereas with most programming based locks, you can't do that, and just gluing things together will break concurrency if you get it wrong... and breaking concurrency is usually extremely difficult to test for.
  5. DBs are magical in that they both guarantee incredibly robust concurrency (Serializable transaction isolation in essence means: It's as if all code ran single threaded, including the acts of witnessing data and such), whilst still having great performance. At least, most DBs can do this (such as postgres).
  6. It keeps your java-side webserver endpoint code simple and independent: All your endpoint runners don't need to even think about the fact that it is running on a webserver that is accessed concurrently. (Because all concurrency control is done at the DB level).

The big downside is that, whatever DB interaction you have, it MUST be ready for this model. This means that you must catch the retry exceptions and do what it says (retry the block). The retry is how DB engines do the magical act (be fast and concurrent at the same time): Optimistic locking. This means all your db-interacting code needs to be:

  1. In a context such that the framework can rerun it. For JDBI and JOOQ or raw JDBC this means in lambda blocks so that the framework can rerun it. For frameworks like spring, in a method annotated with e.g. @Transactional so that spring will re-start your method.
  2. Must be idempotent. There must be no observable difference between calling your method once, twice, or a hundred times, even if some of those runs exit halfway through running.

It's the better way to write such software but if you have a large project that wasn't written with the two caveats in mind, oof. That's a real problem. But, you mentioned spring, presumably you do have @Transactional on the relevant methods already. So then it's just the 'idempotent' part.

Once you've done that your actual question is moot: You don't need any locks in your JVM code.
